extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature/drama; playwrights and critics studying Aristotle's Poetics and tragic form
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama: criteria for the ideal tragic hero, acceptable/forbidden character-types, and the plot-structures that produce tragic pity and fear. Emphasises Aristotelian concepts (hamartia, peripeteia) and their interpretation in later drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of the perfectly blameless character (ἐπιεικής)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ἐπιεικής or perfectly blameless character is deemed unfit to be a tragic hero on the ground that wholly unmerited suffering causes repulsion, not fear or pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's rationale: wholly unmerited suffering expels pity because it provokes admiration or a sense of outraged justice rather than sympathetic pity ('Si vis me flere dolendum est primum ipsi tibi'). Lessing and others debate this, but the practical consequence for drama is to avoid centring tragedy on a character whose virtue is so unassailable that their suffering fails to elicit the proper tragic emotions. Example/discussion: Antigone described as 'sinless crime' yet raises interpretive difficulties; the author questions Aristotle's absolute rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prosperity of the wicked (no triumph of wickedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'bad man who is raised from adverse to prosperous fortune' is 'most alien to the spirit of tragedy' because prosperity following bad actions offends the sense of justice and fails to arouse pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representations in which wickedness triumphs reproduce life but disrupt the aesthetic harmony expected in drama; they tend to awaken disquiet or disbelief rather than the tragic union of pity and terror. The text treats such outcomes as to be 'rigorously excluded' from tragedy (and from art generally), because they suspend the operation of moral law and introduce caprice or blind chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial or purely unselfish goodness as protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Blameless goodness often lacks the motive power and self-assertive energy required for dramatic interest; 'goodness... is apt to be immobile and uncombative' and may bring action to a standstill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic character requires initiative and the capacity to impel others and create collisions of will. Purely self-effacing virtue tends not to generate decisive acts of will or conflict; such characters rarely sustain tragic action. Practical implication: protagonists should possess qualities that engage conflict, not only moral purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero must be a 'man like ourselves' (ὅμοιος) with mixed elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal protagonist is composed of mixed elements — not supremely good, but a man 'like ourselves' who is elevated in power or feeling yet shares common humanity; he falls from lofty eminence and his disaster stems from some great error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read Aristotle in context: the tragic hero should be sympathetic because of his humanity, but also elevated enough (in power, intellect, or feeling) to make the fall striking. Examples: Oedipus, Othello, Hamlet, Macbeth, Lear; the hero's mixture of strength and weakness elicits pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (ἁμαρτία) — the tragic error/frailty
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's downfall should be due to a significant ἁμαρτία — variously: an error of judgment (due to inadequate knowledge), an unavoidable misfortune (ἀτύχημα), or a defect of character — typically an unintentional error or frailty rather than deliberate vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term admits several shades: (a) error due to ignorance of particulars (could have been avoided), (b) misfortune/unavoidable ignorance, (c) a character-defect that is not vicious. The moral culpability affects the ethical reading but all forms can generate pity. Examples and notes: Oedipus (series of errors culminating unconsciously in marriage to his mother); Macbeth (ambition that grows into crime); Hamlet/Othello as variations where defect or error produces ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality and unity: the first error must bear the weight of the tragic result
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the plot bring together beginning and end so that 'the first ἁμαρτία bears the weight of the tragic result' — the causal chain should unite the whole action so the initial mistake is implicit in the catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great tragedy shows how a frailty or initial false step grows into crime and culminates in disaster; the intervening process should disappear in a well-unified causal sequence. The plot should make the end implicit in the beginning, not appear arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as primary element: prefer 'complicated' plots with peripeteia (περιπέτεια)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (μῦθος) holds first place among the elements of tragedy; the ideal is the 'complicated' (πεπλεγμένη) plot characterized by περιπέτεια — a sudden reversal of fortune brought about by the very means which seemed adapted to produce the contrary effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle privileges plots that represent action (inner processes realized outwardly) including fortune and misfortune. Example: Oedipus Tyrannus, where means meant to prove innocence become proof of guilt. Practical implication: structure scenes so that the reversal is ironical and causally motivated by earlier actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must produce the tragic effect by reading as well as by staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle requires a good tragedy to produce its proper effect merely by reading; reliance solely on stage representation and acting is a limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While powerful stage effect is acknowledged (Euripides 'tragic' on stage if acting and representation are adequate), the highest standard is a work whose tragic power survives the text alone. This implies tightness of structure, clarity of causal logic, and intrinsic emotional force in the writing itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should arouse pity and fear (pathos and terror) in high degree
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal tragedy will excite pity and fear in no ordinary combination, but these emotions heightened to their utmost capacity under conditions of perfect art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combination and intensification of these emotions is central to tragic effect; plays that fail to evoke both will fall short of the tragic idea. The text notes modern literature (Shakespeare) enlarges how hamartia produces such effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simply showing the overthrow of signal villainy as central interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The overthrow of conspicuous villainy is unsuited to tragedy because deserved suffering does not inspire pity and the villain is often too remote from the audience to evoke fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, exceptions exist: 'wickedness on a grand scale, resolute and intellectual, may raise the criminal above the commonplace' and produce tragic sympathy through a sense of wasted greatness or grandeur (e.g., Richard III, Iago to different effects). If depicting villainy, give it imposing scale, dignity or intellectual mastery to render it dramatically powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different kinds of tragic collision: external fate vs internal moral struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic collision can be (a) man against forces outside him (fate or other wills), often beginning unwittingly, or (b) a conflict of internal moral forces — struggles of conscience, wavering purpose, divided will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both types can produce tragedy; Aristotle's scheme accommodates unwitting error leading to fate-driven ruin as well as character-driven moral collisions (the latter more prominent in Euripides and modern drama). Playwrights should decide which collision best serves the plot and tragic intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: The tragic hero ought to be elevated in power or feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond being 'like ourselves,' the tragic hero should be 'raised above the ordinary level' especially in power, depth of feeling, or heightened intellect/will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere moral mediocrity is insufficient; the protagonist's elevated capacities make the fall meaningful and awe-inspiring. This heightening contributes to grandeur and the magnitude of the tragic experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martyrdom and moral victory are not the same as tragic defeat
rubrics_metrics.description: The death of the martyr or of a benefactor who bears suffering to achieve moral victory 'fills us with wonder and admiration' but 'can hardly produce the thrill of fear or tragic awe' essential to true tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the protagonist's suffering is primarily a moral triumph aligned with higher powers, the audience's response tends toward admiration rather than the mixed pity-and-fear of tragedy. Use martyrdom cautiously if the aim is tragic, not purely moral exemplarhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character is subordinate to plot but must be 'well marked' and consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle places ἦθος (character) after plot; characters must be convincing, 'mixed', and able to realize action, but they are evaluated in terms of what they do within the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be sharply drawn ('well marked' as commentators argue) so they contribute causally to the plot; avoid caricatured virtue or vice that cannot plausibly drive the action. Examples of interplay: pairs of contrasting characters (Antigone/Ismene, Hamlet/Laertes) illustrate the law of light and shade required for dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of cause and effect to satisfy the rational faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: In drama 'our view of the universe needs to be harmonised' — the plot should present cause-and-effect connections that satisfy reason; suspending moral law by having wickedness triumph introduces caprice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aesthetic effect depends on intelligible causal structure; the audience expects a form where causes relate to effects in a way that restores order (moral or cosmic). This supports the requirement for a coherent peripeteia and well-justified outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing Aristotle's rules dogmatically; allow scope for variation
rubrics_metrics.description: While Aristotle sketches the 'ideal tragedy', his remarks are tentative and allusive; his rules describe what is best, not an absolute code for all times and forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and dramatists should adapt the principles rather than apply them rigidly; Shakespearean examples demonstrate enlargement of hamartia and types of tragic portraiture beyond a strict Aristotelian reading. Practical advice: use Aristotelian standards as guiding ideals, not absolute constraints.
